steps: Unpack & check the parts
Inspect the stove and all parts for shipping damage; report damaged or missing parts to the dealer. Remove the packaging in the flue collar before installing the chimney.

• Pack list: stove, owner's manual, parts box. A separate box under the stove holds internal parts, with its own instruction sheet.
  • The label hangs on a cable under the stove — don't damage it when lifting. After final positioning it can be stored in the holding clip on the bottom shield.
Site & floor protection

Freestanding room heater only — never in a factory-built fireplace. Over a combustible floor, a noncombustible protector of at least 33 1/4in x 33-1/2in (US) or 42in x 43 1/2in (Canada); no insulated hearth pad needed.

Choose a main living area rather than a basement or confined space, away from traffic flow, doors and hallways, and never in or near a storage area for gasoline, kerosene or other flammable liquids. Check clearances to walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase before connecting.

US minimum33 1/4in x 33-1/2in
Canada minimum42in x 43 1/2in

A continuous layer of tile, brick, slate, glass or other noncombustible facing qualifies; there is no R-value requirement. How far it must extend past the stove is shown only in Figure 3. Some luxury vinyl plank or tile begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit — check the flooring maker's limit; extra shielding may be needed.
Clearances to combustibles
Set the stove to the Figure 4 table for your connector and shield (letters A–F, measured from the stove body). Alcove: minimum width 52", ceiling at least 61.5" from the floor.

The full table is under the Clearances spec. Double-wall values are specific to Simpson DuraVent DVL. A rear connector pipe must be UL listed; check its listing for clearances. Clearances may be reduced with an NFPA 211 approved wall protection system, with approval of the local authority.
Outside air kit (optional)

Kit 96-53400 connects the stove's air intake to a minimum 3" (76 mm) duct (adaptor for 4" duct: kit 90-53308). Required in all mobile home installations; in Canada the stove must then be fastened to the floor.

• The kit attaches to the underside of the stove; follow the kit's own instructions and route the duct around structural members.
  • The IRC does not allow the duct to terminate higher than the appliance. Hearthstone recommends terminating at the same level as, or lower than, the stove's air intake.
  • Locate the termination where snow, leaves or other material can't block it. Screen it with ¼" x ¼" mesh rodent screen and cover it with a rain/wind proof hood (supplied by others).
  • Canada: fasten the stove to the subfloor with the shipping clips and long enough fasteners.
Chimney connector

6" (152 mm) 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel, crimped ends toward the stove, three #10 x 1/2" sheet metal screws per joint, horizontal runs rising at least 1/4" per foot. Never through a floor, ceiling, attic, closet or concealed space.

• No aluminum or galvanized pipe. A double-wall connector reduces clearances with a listed Type HT or masonry chimney (e.g. Simpson Dura Vent DVL, Metalbestos DS; Security, GSW and Ameritec are also acceptable).
  • Keep the run as short and straight as possible; extra length and elbows add draft resistance and creosote. A cleanout tee is recommended.
  • Through a combustible wall, use a wall thimble or pass-through per NFPA Code 211 or CAN/CSA-B365; four pass-through systems are described on p. 12.
  • Never connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution duct, and don't use stovepipe as a chimney.
Chimney

A listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved masonry chimney with a flue liner. 6" inside diameter for new installations; an existing 8" flue can be used with a reducer.

• Size: not less than the flue collar, and not more than three times its cross-sectional area. An oversized flue builds creosote.
  • Prefab: follow the chimney maker's instructions precisely and buy the pass-through, "T" section, fire-stops, insulation shield, flashing and cap from the same maker. Choose an interior chimney whenever possible.
  • Masonry: have a professional check it for cracks, loose mortar, deterioration and blockage, and repair it first; the cleanout door must seal tightly. Brick or block at least 4" (102 mm) thick, or rubble/stone, always lined — tile (5/8" (16 mm) wall, refractory mortar, 1" (25 mm) air space) or UL listed 6" stainless steel, insulated or wrapped.
  • Clearance to combustibles: interior chimney at least 2" (51 mm), exterior at least 1" (25 mm).
Chimney height & draft

At least 3 feet above the roof opening and 2 feet above any roof within 10 feet. Recommended minimum 16 feet off the floor (top exit) or 19 feet (rear exit), maximum 30 feet. Check the draft at installation.

A tall chimney can create higher than normal draft; install a stovepipe damper when the draft is above 0.1" WC. Some installations need more than one damper.

Note: p. 15 gives the required draft as 0.06" to 0.1" WC; p. 16 gives 0.08" to 0.15" water column.
Mobile home (if applicable)
Install per 24 CFR, Part 3280 (HUD) with the outside air kit, the stove permanently fastened to the floor, and a listed mobile home chimney & connector kit. Never in a sleeping room.

• Fasten the stove to the subfloor with the shipping clips and long enough fasteners.
  • The kit (US/UL103 or CAN/ULC-S629) must include a stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes and a 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof, and the vapor barrier where the chimney exits.
  • Remove the chimney when transporting the home.
First fires: break-in

The first fire, and the first fire each season, is a small warm-not-hot fire to season the soapstone and cure the furnace cement. Inspect, and clean if needed, the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is complete.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → open the primary air fully one minute before opening the door; make sure the bypass is open
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window in the stove room
Blocked chimney → check chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Oversized chimney → reline to the right diameter; undersized → draft inducer or new chimney; too short → lengthen
Bypass not closed → close it once the catalysts are in the active range
Catalysts not working → inspect for damage, ash or plugging; brush or vacuum lightly, replace if needed
More than one appliance on the flue → disconnect the others and seal openings

panels.title: Back-puffing
items: Operating technique → air fully open one minute before opening the door and for a few minutes after reloading; bypass open before the door
Extra-low burn rate → burn at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty ashes more often; avoid poor-quality or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door → close it tightly or replace the gaskets; replace a leaking glass gasket
Excessive draft → check the installation, run at low burn; correct draft in excess of 0.1 wc with stovepipe damper(s)
Extra-long chimney → shorten it or add stovepipe damper(s)
Oversized chimney → reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Poor-quality, low-Btu or green wood → air-dried wood, preferably dried at least one year
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney → reline or insulate it
Leaky stovepipe or chimney → check the installation; insulated prefab or properly sized masonry chimney
Too much heat loss from the house → insulation, efficient windows, caulking and sealing
Excessive ash build-up → empty ashes more often

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
This is the everyday start. For the stove's very first fire, and the first fire of each season, do a gentle break-in fire instead.

  1. Open the bypass: handle pointed toward the front of the stove.
  2. Open the front door. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox.
  3. Lay about 10 pieces of kindling, 1/2" in diameter and 10" to 16" long, in a tee-pee over the paper.
  4. Pull the primary air lever all the way out (fully open).
  5. Light the paper under the kindling. Leave the door open a crack for a moment, until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull.
  6. Close the door and let it burn.
  7. Once the kindling is burning, open the door and add logs, small ones first. Keep them away from the glass.
  8. When the catalyst thermometer reads Active, close the bypass (handle toward the rear).
  9. Let it run on high for about 20 minutes, then use the air lever to set the burn you want.
Build the fire right on the firebox floor, with no grate, and toward the center so coals don't pile up against the glass.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire. Keep the door closed while the stove is burning.

breakin.title: Breaking in your stove
breakin.html:
Soapstone has to be seasoned. The moisture in new stone must come out slowly, and the furnace cement must cure slowly. Over-firing a new stove can crack the soapstone. Build your first fire, and the first fire of every season, like this:

  1. Open the bypass. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox, with about ten pieces of kindling in a crisscross on top.
  2. Pull the primary air control fully open, toward you.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door open a crack for a moment until the kindling catches, then close the door.
  4. Keep a watchful eye on it. You want a steady, low-heat fire: the stove should get warm, but not hot to the touch. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  5. Once it's warm but not hot, push the air control fully in and let the fire die out.
  6. Let the stove cool back to room temperature.
Visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot.

Smoke and smells at first are normal

Paints and oils give off smoke and fumes during the first fires. Open a few windows; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes and ends once the stove is cured. Break-in fires can dirty the glass and build creosote quickly, so look over the stovepipe and chimney afterward.

controls.title: Air, bypass & thermometer
controls.html:
Learn these before your first fire, and wear fireplace gloves when the stove is hot.

Front door

Pull up on the wood handle and swing the door open. To latch it, push the door tightly toward the firebox, then push the handle in and down until it latches. Give it a gentle pull to check.

Primary air lever

It sits under the ash lip. Pull it out for more air and a faster, hotter fire; push it in for a slower burn. It never closes completely.

Bypass handle

The catalyst burns up smoke once it's hot. The bypass decides whether smoke goes around it or through it.

  • Pointed to the front: open. Use it when starting a fire and every time before you open the door.
  • Pointed to the rear: closed. Close it once the catalyst is up to temperature, and leave it closed while the stove burns in the active range.

Catalyst thermometer

Inactivebypass open until the stove heats up
Activeclose the bypass
Too Hotkeep the door closed, push the air fully in, let it cool to Active

The stove typically runs between 800 °F and 1300 °F.

burn.title: Reloading & burn rates
burn.html:
Reloading

  1. Open the bypass first, every time.
  2. Open the door just a crack and pause so the smoke clears, then open it fully.
  3. Load onto a bed of hot, red coals. Leave a small valley in the coals behind the Lower Primary Air Opening so the new wood lights faster.
  4. If the fire had cooled or burned down to charcoal, run medium to high for about 10 minutes so the catalysts reach approximately 600 °F. Then close the bypass.

To keep creosote down, the manual also says to run with the air fully open for 15 to 20 minutes after reloading.

Burn rates

Lowair lever all the way in
Medium-lowout a little less than 1/4"
Medium-highout a little less than 1/2"
Highall the way out

Medium-low is the typical setting, and the best one when you leave the stove unattended. Don't burn on low for long stretches, because it builds creosote. Once or twice a day, run it on high for 35 to 45 minutes to fully heat the stovepipe and chimney.

The lowest burn rate is set at the factory. Federal rules forbid changing it.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood). The stove isn't designed for any other fuel.

  • Dry is what matters most. Seasoned firewood is at or near 20% moisture. A hand-held moisture meter from a hearth shop will tell you.
  • Season green wood: split it, stack it and let it air-dry for a year. Stack it on skids or blocks and cover only the top; tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Hardwoods burn longer and leave better coals; softwoods burn hotter and faster. In the manual's heat-content chart, sugar maple, red oak, white ash and yellow birch rank "medium high."
  • Logs up to 18" long fit the firebox.
Never burn garbage or trash, coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, painted, treated (including pressure treated) or kiln-dried wood, unseasoned (green) wood, plywood, particleboard, cardboard, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt water saturated materials, flammable fluids, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, or anything other than natural cordwood. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Never use chemicals or flammable fluids to start a fire. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Don't stack firewood inside the stove's clearances, and never put ice-covered wood into a burning stove.

ash.title: Removing ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, or sooner if the firebox is full.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely. You can leave a thin layer of ash in the firebox.
  2. Push large live coals to the side and scoop out only the finer ash with a fireplace shovel.
  3. Don't let ash build up around the door opening. It can spill out, or pack into the gasket channel and stop the door sealing.

Storing the ashes

  • Put them straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Nothing else goes in it, and don't pour water in.
  • Set the closed container on a noncombustible floor or outside on the ground, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles. Never set it on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring; it can be hot.
  • Keep the ashes in the closed container until every coal is cold, including before you bury or spread them.
Coals in a bed of ashes can stay hot for several days. Never use wooden or plastic containers, trash cans, or paper or plastic bags, no matter how long the fire has been out.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Clean the glass only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the inside of the glass in circles.
  2. When the deposits are gone, clean up with window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner (the same on the outside), following the cleaner's directions.
  3. Wipe it off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
Note: p. 29 suggests window cleaner or stove-glass cleaner for the glass, then p. 30 says to use only a cleaner made specifically for woodstoves.

Never use a razor blade, steel wool or anything abrasive; scratches weaken the glass. If the glass always stays dirty, your fires are too cool or the wood is wet, which also means more creosote.

Cracked or chipped glass

Don't use the stove until the glass is replaced. It's a special ceramic glass, so use only the glass kit (96-58607) from your dealer.

Note: p. 28 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass; p. 30 gives advice for replacing it yourself (work gloves, safety glasses).

care.title: Chimney & catalyst checks
care.html:
Every other month

  • Look over the chimney connector and chimney for creosote, the tar that slow, cool fires leave in the flue. If it catches fire it burns extremely hot.
  • Dollar-bill test: with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, the door isn't sealing. Adjust the latch or replace the door gasket.
  • Check the face of the catalyst for fly ash and soot and brush it off with a soft-bristled brush. Inspect the catalyst at least 3 times a heating season.

End of every season

  • Take apart and clean the chimney connector; replace rusted pieces.
  • Inspect the chimney and clean it if needed. Clean out the inside of the stove.
  • Check and clean the catalyst. Replace door gasket that is worn, frayed, cracked or very hard.

Creosote

Until you learn your stove, check for creosote daily. If it is building up, check at least monthly, and have it removed once it's more than 1/8" thick; a certified chimney sweep is recommended. Have the whole system professionally inspected before each heating season.

Plan on a new door gasket every two to three seasons, using a Hearthstone gasket kit from your dealer.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a chimney fire

  1. If it's threatening, leave and call the fire department right away.
  2. If not: close the primary air control, close the stovepipe damper (if you have one), close the bypass, and keep the front door closed.
  3. Once it's out, leave the air control and bypass closed and let the stove's fire die out. Inspect the stove, stovepipe and chimney, and fix any damage before you light it again.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney. It turns to steam instantly and can cause serious injury.

Signs of over-firing

Never over-fire your stove. It damages the stove. Over-firing means running hotter than a normal high burn. Watch for warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, or a discolored stovepipe. If you suspect it's over-firing, stop using the stove and call your dealer immediately. Over-firing damage isn't covered, and any sign of it voids the warranty.

Every day

  • The stove is hot while it runs. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away, and keep combustibles at least 36" from it.
  • Put smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) detectors throughout the home, including bedrooms and hallways, and keep an "A B C" fire extinguisher handy.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone's limited warranty covers the original retail purchaser only, on a stove installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their representative. It starts on the original invoice date and isn't transferable. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone, cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles & latches, steel components & firebox5 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, all components not listed elsewhere1 year

Other parts are marked by fuel type in a grid; check it in the manual. Hearthstone pays first-year labor on dealer-installed stoves, and parts shipping for 90 days.

Note: the coverage grid lists glass at 1 year (p. 37), but the exclusions list glass among wear parts that aren't covered (p. 38).

Catalysts

Covered by Applied Ceramics: free replacement within two (2) years (send the original bill of sale and the old combustor; no abuse or wrong fuels), then Year 3 $130.00, Year 4 $140.00, Year 5 $150.00, Year 6 $160.00, and current retail after that.

Note: p. 36 gives the free catalyst replacement period as two (2) years, then refers to "the three year period."

Not covered: over-firing, other fuels, water damage, unapproved changes, wear parts, expansion noise, odors. Claims go through your dealer; registering is optional.

specOutput.title: Heat output
specOutput.html:
Maximum heat output60,000 BTUs per hour of cordwood
Heated areaUp to a maximum of 2,000 square feet
Burn timeUp to 24+ hrs. (Heat Life™: Up to 30 hours)
Maker's website: HeatLife 24 Hours of heat.

The 60,000 figure is based on independent laboratory test results with cordwood. Under EPA test conditions (crib wood) the stove delivered 12,600 to 33,600 Btu (output); see Efficiency & emissions. Insulation, windows, floor plan, stove placement and fuel quality can reduce the area heated. Wood per cubic foot of firebox varies from 10 to 25 lbs. with species, moisture and packing density.

specCat.title: Catalytic combustor
specCat.html:
CatalystACI-6M2, Applied Ceramics FIRECAT STEEL
Becomes activearound 500 °F (260°C)
Typical operating range800 °F to 1300 °F
Replacement kit96-75400
Catalyst thermometer7200-520

Cold start: hold a medium to high firing rate for about 20 minutes. Never operate without the catalysts; it is against federal regulations to operate this heater with the catalytic element deactivated or removed. Inspect at least three times a heating season.

Service (pp. 25–27)

Face inspection: with stove and ashes cool, remove the baffle protector and baffles and brush or vacuum the catalyst face. Removal is from the back: loosen (don't remove) the rear heat shield screws if a shield is fitted, slide the shield off, remove the 2 bolts and the cast iron catalyst access cover, then lift the catalysts off the ribs and out. Clean with compressed air under 35 psi or a hot (not boiling) soak of 4 parts water to 1 part vinegar; no metal tools, detergents or chemicals. Re-gasket if the old catalysts had gasket, then heat slowly on the next fire. Acceptable warping limits are shown only in a figure (p. 27).

Catalyst faults (p. 33)

  • Fly ash build-up → light-off temperature not maintained, char-heavy materials (cardboard, gift wrap, garbage), or bypass closed too soon
  • Plugging or masking → wet, pitchy wood, or large loads of small diameter wood without light-off; build a hot fire, close the bypass only when well in range, run hot for one hour
  • Warping or bowing → too hot for long periods; reduce the air setting

Warranty grid (p. 37): only rows marked X X X (all three fuel columns) are transcribed; rows with one or two X marks (clean burning air supply system, burner and logs, burn pot and baffles, refractory/vermiculite panels/baffles, ash grate) can't be assigned to a fuel column from the text, so owners are pointed to the grid. Heat output: 60,000 BTUs per hour maximum with cordwood (p. 7) vs 12,600 to 33,600 Btu under EPA crib-wood test conditions (p. 2); different stated bases, both shown, not flagged as a conflict. Break-in kindling is printed 10" to 16" (254 mm to 457 mm) on p. 22 while the everyday fire says 254 mm to 406 mm; the guide uses inches only. Troubleshooting (p. 32) says to empty the 'ash pan' and p. 24 mentions 'ash doors', while ash removal (p. 24) describes shoveling from the firebox; the guide says 'empty ashes'. p. 20 says unauthorized fuel such as coal can produce high levels of carbon dioxide, p. 18 says carbon monoxide; the guide repeats neither. p. 29 recommends full air for 15 to 20 minutes after reloading while p. 23 says medium to high for about 10 minutes for a cool fire; both shown in the burn drawer with their contexts.
